data.title: Oil notches first weekly gain in November on supply fears
data.description:
[HOUSTON] Brent crude edged down on Friday (Nov 27), but snapped a three-week losing streak to notch its first weekly gain in November, as attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and Saudi energy infrastructure fanned concerns over Middle East supplies.

Brent crude futures fell US$1.13 or 1.2 per cent to US$95.44 a barrel. It hit its highest since Nov 9 earlier in the session, but stayed shy of the US$100 mark.

US West Texas Intermediate crude futures settled at US$83.08 a barrel down US$0.60 or 0.7 per cent from Wednesday’s close. There was no Thursday settlement for WTI because of the US Thanksgiving holiday.

Brent gained about 3 per cent on the week, while WTI lost 0.9 per cent.

“Attacks on Middle Eastern energy facilities and tankers have brought supply disruption back into focus,” said Mark Schaefer, a director at brokerage Liquidity Energy.

Prices retreated in recent weeks as investors were relieved that US President Donald Trump did not step up military action against Iran after the midterm elections.

However, Iran has continued to attack ships transiting the key Strait of Hormuz, disrupting oil exports, while Yemen’s Houthis have struck Saudi Arabian infrastructure.

The US military said on Friday it disabled a commercial ship on Thursday after it attempted to run the US blockade of Iran, while an adviser to the Iranian supreme leader said Iran would keep the Strait of Hormuz shut while vowing to break the embargo.

Saudi Aramco’s Jazan refinery temporarily halted some operations after a projectile struck it on Thursday, killing a worker, Saudi Arabia’s Energy Ministry said. The strike was the latest blow to key Saudi facilities, a day after the Houthis claimed attacks on Ras Tanura, the kingdom’s largest refinery and a major crude export hub.

Opec+, which includes Saudi Arabia and Russia, is set to keep first-quarter 2027 output targets unchanged when the group meets on Sunday, three people with knowledge of the talks said.

Separately, 10 people familiar with the matter told Reuters that the US administration encouraged Venezuela and Iraq to consider leaving Opec earlier this year and blocked Venezuela from paying its membership dues.

Iraq is in negotiations with Opec to raise its production ceiling as the country looks to develop its energy sector, oil minister Basim Mohammed Khudair said on Friday ahead of the Opec+ meeting.

“We think Brent can still push above US$100 a barrel without another major escalation in the Middle East, but that increasingly requires evidence of constrained deliverable supply,” ANZ analysts Brian Martin and Daniel Hynes said in a research note.

Ukraine has intensified drone attacks on Russian oil refineries since the end of October, with the latest incident causing a fire at the Slavyansk ECO refinery in Russia’s southern region of Krasnodar.

Separately, fires disrupted activity at Thailand’s Bangchak refinery and Venezuela’s Amuay refinery on Thursday. REUTERS

data.title: Europe: Shares log strong weekly gains; markets await Spanish election
data.description:
[BENGALURU] Europe’s benchmark share index closed at a one-week high on Friday (Nov 27) after broad sectoral gains, as investors bought riskier assets following steep losses earlier this month.

Investors’ attention now turns to Spain’s election on Sunday.

The pan-European Stoxx 600 gained 1 per cent to 643.85 points. It gained nearly 3 per cent on the week, its sharpest weekly rise since mid-May, bouncing back from the steepest weekly decline since late March 2025.

“There doesn’t seem to be any firm catalyst behind the bounce that we’ve seen, but it has been a very bruising month. What we’re seeing here is dip buyers coming in,” said Fiona Cincotta, senior market analyst at StoneX.

Equities were rebounding from what has been a bruising month for artificial intelligence-exposed global stocks as investors grew frustrated with returns on debt-backed AI investments and a brief leadership crisis at chip giant Nvidia.

On Friday, however, European technology stocks added 2 per cent, led by semiconductor shares ASML, ASM International and Infineon, which gained between 2 and 2.7 per cent. For the week, the index was 1 per cent higher.

Mining stocks jumped more than 3.5 per cent as copper and gold prices rose. Fresnillo and Pan African Resources rose more than 4 per cent each.

Defence stocks also gained, with Rheinmetall up 3.3 per cent after a report on a planned AI-platform partnership with Deutsche Telekom.

The broader aerospace and defence index climbed 2 per cent after Bloomberg News reported the European Union was planning new funds to replace US war-fighting capabilities.

The spotlight will now be on Sunday’s snap election in Spain, called by Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez after parliament rejected housing measures aimed at tackling a crisis that has triggered protests across the country.

Alberto Nunez Feijoo’s centre-right People’s Party is leading in polls ahead of the vote, although most suggest he will have to form a coalition with far-right Vox to secure a parliamentary majority.

The vote could be a gauge of public sentiment ahead of pivotal elections in France and Italy that also witnessed similar protests, at a time when investors are sensitive to the massive debt pile of developed economies.

“With fiscal policy set to be tightened again and uncertainty likely to spike around the presidential elections, growth will probably be very weak again in 2027,” Andrew Kenningham, chief Europe economist at Capital Economics, said on France.

Investors, meanwhile, shrugged off the Trump administration’s move to propose tariffs on goods from the EU.

Consumer-facing foods and beverages slipped 0.3 per cent, with sportswear makers Adidas and Puma flat and down about 1 per cent, respectively.

Data this week showed US inflation rose further last month, and the economy grew more than previously expected, adding to bets on interest rate hikes.

Among others, Thales gained 2.3 per cent after French laser technology company Lumibird said it had entered exclusive talks to sell a controlling stake to the defence group. Lumibird surged 18.1 per cent. REUTERS

data.title: US: Wall Street ends higher as battered AI stocks gain in volatile week
data.description:
[NEW YORK] Wall Street’s main indices ended higher on Friday (Nov 27) and posted weekly gains as investors returned from the Thanksgiving holiday and flocked to hard-hit artificial intelligence-linked shares.

US stocks have swung sharply this week, with Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia CEO and Anthropic’s brief fall below its initial public offering price adding to volatility across the AI trade.

Investors have alternated between bargain-hunting after a steep sell-off and fretting over soaring AI costs, heavy borrowing and doubts about companies’ returns on investment.

“The market is so oversold that a bounce was inevitable,” said Jamie Cox, managing partner at Harris Financial Group.

Chipmakers that investors battered this month recovered ground, with Micron and Marvell gaining 7.6 per cent and 7.3 per cent, respectively. The broader chip gauge also climbed 4.7 per cent. Nvidia, after remaining weak for most of the session, ended 0.8 per cent higher.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 591.99 points or 1.2 per cent to 50,774.94, the S&P 500 gained 114.71 points or 1.6 per cent to 7,297.49, and the Nasdaq Composite gained 543.70 points or 2.3 per cent to 24,129.5.

AI beneficiaries, including data-storage firm Sandisk, surged almost 16 per cent, while optical-products maker Lumentum and server maker Dell also gained sharply.

AI hyperscalers – tech companies that run large data centres – also rose, with Amazon.com, Microsoft, Meta Platforms and Oracle posting gains. Tesla surged 5 per cent.

“There is a bounce in technology which started Monday, continued Wednesday with an intraday reversal and now continues today. So much fast money has delevered out of tech that this could have persistence next week as they are forced to chase back in,” said Andrew Slimmon, senior portfolio manager at Morgan Stanley Investment Management.

Weekly gains

For the week, the S&P 500 gained 5.6 per cent, the Nasdaq rose 6.7 per cent, and the Dow climbed 5.5 per cent. The S&P 500 weekly gain was the index’s biggest since April 2025.

The S&P 500 bank index rose 1.6 per cent, fuelled by JPMorgan Chase’s almost 2 per cent gain.

The market’s gains have done little to erase November’s losses. The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq are on track for their worst November since 2008, pressured by concerns over tougher AI regulation following the Democrats’ US midterm election victory and expectations that monetary policy will remain restrictive.

Traders are almost fully pricing in a Federal Reserve interest rate hike in December after data this week showed the US economy grew much faster than initially estimated in the third quarter and inflation accelerated further in October.

Gold and silver miners rallied as precious-metal prices recovered from a bruising few sessions. Newmont gained 5.4 per cent, while the Global X Silver Miners ETF also advanced.

Vertex Pharmaceuticals slid 5.2 per cent after the US Food and Drug Administration extended its review of the company’s kidney-disease drug by up to three months.

US equity markets were open for a half-day session on Friday, following Thursday’s Thanksgiving holiday.

Volume on US exchanges was 10.97 billion shares.

Advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 3.25-to-1 ratio on the NYSE. There were 55 new highs and 73 new lows on the NYSE.

On the Nasdaq, 3,677 stocks rose and 1,135 fell as advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 3.24-to-1 ratio.

The S&P 500 posted 12 new 52-week highs and no new lows, while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 53 new highs and 96 new lows. REUTERS

data.title: Audi RS 5 Avant review: The dragon wagon with a feature for the heroic
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The Audi RS 5 Avant is the car I’d love to drive to a dinner party at which someone is blathering on that their electric saloon can spank a Ferrari in a straight line.

You’d think any performance junkie would be thrilled that today’s fast battery-powered car is quicker than yesterday’s combustion hero. 

But the truth is, the silent, brutishly powerful electric vehicle has a way of sucking the joy out of fast car discussions, maybe because they tend to be driven by the only thing worse than a car bore (namely, an EV bore), or maybe because many have names that sound like Wi-Fi passwords.

But here comes an Audi to lift the keen driver’s soul.

Men stare enviously at its sculpted frame. Its bulged haunches make it look like something from the German touring car championship, though they’re there because of the wider tracks and tweaked suspension responsible for its impressive stability.

And not only does it have a drift mode, it also comes with a display that measures how big your tail slides are and how long you can hold them, if you’re heroic enough to use it.

Speaking of heroes, red paint makes the RS 5 Avant resemble Spider-Man, not least because of its comically oversized front grille. But the huge openings don’t merely make the Audi look like it could swallow naughty children whole.

I counted at least seven radiators or heat exchangers under the bonnet, so clearly the powertrain wants cool air, and plenty of it.

In truth, this fiery Audi straddles both combustion and electric realms. It’s the first plug-in hybrid EV (PHEV) from Audi’s high-performance RS label.

Though it packs 639 horsepower (hp), only 510 of that is from a twin-turbo V6 engine. An electric motor tucked inside the gearbox adds 177 hp, drawing power from a 22 kwh battery concealed inside the boot.

The upshot of the PHEV set-up? The Audi can pootle along electrically for up to 84 km. You can park it in EV charging spots. It might even be better for the environment than a regular car, assuming you take pains to charge it every day.

But if you’re anything like me, you’ll drive it 90 per cent of the time in dynamic mode. That keeps the engine running and holds the battery level at 20 per cent or more so it can unleash the full force of the powertrain.

Roused into action this way, the V6 makes an exquisite din, and when biffing you up the road it doesn’t pull its punches. The punches land hard but precisely, thanks to a new all-wheel drive system that channels power to the outside rear wheel, so the car angles its nose towards the inside of a bend instead of pushing wide.

You do feel the mass of the batteries trying to unsettle the rear at times, but that actually makes the RS 5 more engaging, wiggling slightly like a living thing. Ultimately it still grips hard and stays planted, and before you know it you’re looking up track days at Sepang.

Much as I loved the RS 5, it’s not all roses. The cabin is lovely to look at, but it’s disappointingly cheap-feeling, especially considering that Audi used to make the poshest interiors in the business.

It’s also not as practical as you might expect, because the PHEV batteries leave just 361 litres for cargo. That makes the boot sound tiny, but Germans measure cargo volume only up to seatback height, so there’s still plenty of usable room and you can still fold the rear seats down if you have an Ikea habit.

I’d also call the Audi borderline uncomfortable, even during the neutered calm of EV mode. The suspension is firmer than Superman’s handshake, and the gearbox is tuned for snappy shifts rather than smoothness, so things are sometimes jerky.

You expect that in a car this fast, so the enormous turning circle is my biggest gripe. Some U-turns will make you sweat.

Nevertheless, after returning the RS 5 I wanted to buy a stack of lottery tickets. My chest still aches when I think about how it feels to drive, how it looks and how it sounds. 

I can well imagine someone pointing out that Tesla’s Model 3 Performance is even quicker, and suggesting that only someone with no brain would pay nearly three times as much for the Audi. Maybe, but only someone with no heart would feel that way. Avoid them at dinner parties.

data.title: The portfolio career is not what most people think
data.description:
FOR most of my career, the question “What do you do?” had a fairly straightforward answer. Today, it runs a little longer.

I teach. I consult. I run a merchandise business. I write, and I am working on a book.

At first glance, that looks fragmented. Yet the value lies precisely in the overlap. Consulting gives me real business problems to bring into the classroom. Teaching forces me to explain ideas more clearly.

Writing makes me think harder about what I actually believe. Running a business ensures whatever I say about strategy will actually survive customers, costs and cash flow.

My “portfolio career” is not simply about doing several things but designing them so that each makes the others more valuable.

Start with a core, then build around it

Portfolio careers are often discussed in terms of flexibility or multiple income streams. Those benefits matter, but they undersell the model.

Most successful portfolios need a central piece – an expertise, profession or capability developed deeply enough that other activities can grow around it.

This is why I do not see a portfolio career as a rejection of a conventional one. Years spent inside organisations build expertise, credibility, networks and pattern recognition that can later be deployed in different settings.

What looks like diversification later in life is often built on considerable concentration earlier.

For someone considering this pathway, the first move need not involve resigning. Guest lecturing once a semester, joining a non-profit or industry board, advising a startup, mentoring, writing regularly or taking on a fractional role can all extend existing expertise into new contexts.

You are not starting over. You are finding more ways to use what you have spent years learning.

A portfolio career is also a strategy challenge

In teaching, I often say a good strategy does not just rely on existing strengths; making different choices reinforce one another creates new strength.

A consulting assignment may produce an idea for a lesson. A classroom discussion may sharpen an argument for an article. Writing forces me to structure that argument more rigorously, while running a business provides real-life material that eventually finds its way back into teaching and writing.

The same principle applies when deciding what to add to the portfolio.

Increasingly, I ask three questions: Do I like doing it? Am I good at it? And does it pay well?

“Pay” here is broader than money.

A non-profit board role may offer purpose, governance experience and relationships. Teaching may not compete with a corporate salary, but it sharpens communication and exposes you to younger perspectives.

Writing a book may take years before producing meaningful income, yet it could deepen expertise and open doors elsewhere.

Few activities score perfectly on all three dimensions. A portfolio gives you more room because different roles can provide different returns.

“Less package tour, more independent travel”

Brandon Lee, chief futures at the Skills & Workforce Development Agency and a strong advocate of independent work, has described the future of work as becoming more deconstructed: “Less package tour, more independent travel.”

I like that analogy.

Traditionally, an employer bundled salary, identity, colleagues, training and progression together. Increasingly, experienced professionals can assemble more of those components themselves through different forms of work.

Artificial intelligence lowers the threshold further. Research, writing, analysis and other capabilities that once required substantial organisational infrastructure can increasingly be handled by individuals or small teams.

Yet portfolio work makes something else more obvious: relationships matter.

Knowing how to do good work is necessary, but opportunities often come through people who know, trust and are prepared to recommend you.

AI makes expertise easier to deploy independently, but relationships often determine where that expertise gets deployed.

Meanwhile, the system needs to recognise less conventional forms of work as legitimate contributions. This matters because portfolio careers become much easier to build when employers stop treating every departure from a full-time job as an awkward gap that needs explaining.

Using the optionality you have built

Author and LinkedIn opinion leader Eric Sim, who has 2.8 million followers on the platform, has described the window in life when one has money, time and health at the same time as the “magical stage”.

After a career in banking, Sim now writes, speaks professionally, coaches, and teaches finance.

A portfolio career provides one way to extend the duration of this window. Instead of postponing different interests until retirement, accumulated experience and financial security allow work to be assembled differently.

My own philosophy has become simpler with age: do things I like, or do things with people I like. Even better if I can do things I like with people I like.

A portfolio career allows those different motivations to coexist instead of forcing one job to satisfy all of them.

The real payoff from years spent building “career capital” may not be another title, but greater control over what you do, with whom and why.

Know what not to add

There is, of course, a danger of romanticising all this. Every new commitment consumes attention, often a scarcer resource than time. Four unrelated gigs can simply mean four sets of deadlines.

The harder part may then be deciding what does not belong.

Does a new role deepen something you already do? Does it bring you into contact with people you genuinely want to work with? Does it create knowledge, experience or opportunities that can travel across the rest of your portfolio?

Your answers should guide you.

For much of our careers, success was defined by how far we climbed one ladder. A portfolio career offers a different vantage point.

Like good strategy, the strength of that portfolio will come from how well your choices fit together.

The writer is a former economist who now wears several professional hats. Between guest lecturing and running businesses, he is co-authoring a forthcoming book, The China Mindset.

data.title: The next frontier of Singapore’s urban infrastructure is recovery
data.description:
I HAVE been visiting Singapore regularly for 25 years. As I have aged and evolved, so too has the city. Today, Singapore has reached super-aged status, with more than one in five residents now 65 and above.

This year, the retirement and re-employment ages rose to 64 and 69, respectively; in October, the government confirmed that they will be raised again, to 65 and 70, from 2029 – a year ahead of schedule.

Singapore has always been a forward-thinking city, and while this move is a sound response to the nation’s demographic reality, it raises a question that goes beyond employment policy.

If people are going to live and work longer, what should their cities give back to help them sustain those longer lives? I believe part of the answer lies in an often-overlooked area of urban planning – recovery and well-being infrastructure.

Recovery is not the same as ageing well

Society’s collective thinking around longevity has long centred on healthcare and retirement savings as main support mechanisms for ageing well.

Accordingly, healthy ageing is seen as a long-term outcome, currently measured through lifespan, chronic disease and mobility.

By contrast, recovery is something different altogether. It is the regular, everyday restoration of our physical, mental and social energy. Access to it is what enables a return to a healthy baseline, to combat burnout, and to enjoy productivity in our later years.

If healthy ageing is where we hope to end up, recovery is what we need to do each day; it matters at 25 as much as at 65. Rest is the pause that enables recovery.

This makes recovery a long-term health sustainability issue, not necessarily just a medical one. Nobody can sustain five or six decades of work on will and effort alone. Burnout, chronic stress and poor sleep erode productivity, raise healthcare costs and shorten careers.

Pausing periodically, but without recovering daily, may sometimes give only short-term reprieve. A workforce that needs and wants to stay productive over the long run must be able to recover regularly, and close to home.

From an active city to a restorative city

Across civilisations and through history, human beings have always needed places to gather, recover, bathe, share food, rest, and reconnect with nature and one another.

Take communal bathhouses, saunas and thermal spaces, for example. Beyond the physical experience of heat and water, they enable a break from daily demands and participation in a shared ritual.

Research by the University of Eastern Finland links regular sauna use with better heart health. In today’s context, a bathhouse is also one of the few places where the phone stays in the locker, giving people a reason to come together.

In Japan, the neighbourhood sento has long been a place where grandparents and grandchildren share the same bath; in Budapest, regulars play chess in the steaming outdoor pools of the Szechenyi Thermal Bath, which opened in 1913.

That human connection matters; studies show that people with strong social ties are more likely to have healthier lives and thrive than those without.

Combining water and heat is one approach. Gardens work on the same principles.

NParks’ Therapeutic Garden at West Coast Park, for example, has a sensory path, hands-on planting beds and relaxation zones. It also hosts gardening activities and guided tours with community volunteers.

NParks’ research with the National University of Singapore found that individuals who visited a park during the day were less stressed that evening.

Recovery works best in layers – from small, everyday spaces close to home to larger destinations where people from different generations gather. No single destination can be the whole answer.

What Singapore can do next

The Republic already has strong foundations to build a healthy city. Its planning has long promoted active living and social connection: The park connector network, the hawker centres that serve as the city’s shared living rooms, and more than 230 Active Ageing Centres give older residents places to meet close to home.

Independent bathhouses in Singapore are growing popular, and offer a third space, beyond home and work, for regular access to rest and recovery, particularly for busy professionals.

The is well-placed to further its progress on enabling healthy populations.

Two steps could help: First, design for rest within the spaces Singapore already has. NParks is starting to do this, with invigorating landscapes and more rest points along park connectors. The same thinking could shape community hubs, void decks and new estates, so that quiet corners for recovery sit alongside places to exercise.

Second, build on Healthier SG, which pairs residents with a family doctor and a personal health plan, by encouraging people to include time in parks, gardens and recovery spaces as part of that plan.

Singapore has shown that a city can and should be planned to be liveable. The task now is to plan future cities that support people’s healthspan and recovery.

That means expanding our notion of infrastructure to move beyond hospitals and highways, and to include spots for people to step away from work in order to come back whole, rested and ready to participate.

Rest is not the opposite of productivity, but one of its foundations. A well-functioning city depends on well-functioning people, and Singapore, with its track record of planning ahead, is in a strong position to show the world how to build for both.

The writer is founder and CEO of Therme Group

data.title: Nvidia Blackwell chips turn up at China site tied to Alice Huang
data.description:
A PAIR of Chinese firms installed Nvidia’s powerful Blackwell semiconductors in a Shanghai data centre linked to Alice Huang, the woman at the heart of a controversy surrounding the US chipmaker. 

The gear installed at the Yangtze River Delta Project included a GB300 NVL72 rack, among Nvidia’s most powerful products, according to a serial number specified in documents submitted to Chinese regulators in November.

Shanghai Shuoyao offered the hardware as collateral to obtain a 96 million yuan (US$14 million) loan from Shanghai Innovation Bank, according to filings from the lender that were reviewed by Bloomberg News.

A second firm Shanghai Kezhan, controlled by a Tokyo-based parent, described a GB200 server – which also relies on Blackwell chips – at the facility.

That description was provided in documents when it obtained a 90 million yuan loan in late 2025 from a finance-leasing firm wholly owned by a local Shanghai government agency. 

The submissions reveal for the first time that Nvidia’s Blackwell processors found their way into a Chinese data centre that has ties to Alice Huang and Megaspeed.

These processors were until recently Nvidia’s most powerful data centre products, and they have always been illegal to ship to China without a US licence. 

US President Donald Trump has explicitly said he does not want these chips – which OpenAI and Anthropic use to train their most cutting-edge models – going to the Asian country, at least for now.

Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang, meanwhile, once claimed they were too big to smuggle: a standard 2 m-tall GB300 NVL72 server rack, which contains 72 Blackwell Ultra chips and 36 Grace processors, can weigh more than 1,500 kg and is about the size of a gigantic fridge.

Nvidia and its just-reinstated CEO have come under intense scrutiny in recent weeks for their failure to stop diversion of the company’s products to China, a shadow trade that US officials believe is worth billions of dollars. 

It is unclear how the GB300 rack made its way to the country, to Shanghai Shuoyao or to this specific site – described in local media as designed to house as many as 800,000 servers.

By inputting the serial number for the product into a public warranty database, Bloomberg found that it was manufactured by Taiwan’s Gigabyte Technology, which assembles Nvidia chips into servers and racks.

The database also provided a model name for the serial number, which matches a GB300 NVL72 server rack manufactured by the Taiwanese company. 

This sort of gear often passes through several hands – including local distribution networks – before it is installed in data centres. In many cases, products that were ultimately smuggled into China were originally sold to parties in unrestricted areas. 

Bloomberg provided the rack’s serial number to Gigabyte, seeking information about to whom Gigabyte had originally sold the hardware and when. It declined to answer those questions, citing company policy.

The firm “conducts all business in compliance with applicable laws and regulations”, a spokesperson said in an emailed statement. “All transactions are subject to our internal compliance requirements and the relevant laws and regulations in effect at the time.”

Shanghai Shuoyao – the company that procured the GB300 rack and offered it as collateral – is active at the data centre linked to Alice Huang and also has significant overlap with Singapore-based Megaspeed, which is under US investigation over concerns that it smuggled Nvidia chips to China, Bloomberg has reported.

Shanghai Shuoyao, which has not responded to Bloomberg queries over the past year, confirmed in November in a rare public statement that it is one of Megaspeed’s service providers, describing the partnership as “limited to ordinary commercial cooperation”.

Megaspeed, meanwhile, used a rendering of the Yangtze River Delta Project in 2024 to describe its largest data centre to investors, dubbing the site a “specific area” facility in an unnamed country.

Bloomberg does not have evidence that Megaspeed itself diverted Nvidia hardware there, and Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing in response to the US probe.

The company has not answered repeated queries about the Yangtze River Delta Project. Nor has Nvidia, which for years insisted that there was no black market for its products and did not respond to questions for this story. 

The Trump administration in November put Megaspeed on a US trade blacklist, citing a significant risk of involvement in chip diversion.

Alice Huang in 2023 founded Megaspeed, a so-called neocloud that won a coveted stamp of approval from Nvidia within four days of its creation, and went on to become the chipmaker’s largest South-east Asian customer.

She also has ties to a number of companies that invested in the Yangtze River Delta Project, which counts Kang Wei as its president. Kang has been introduced at times as Alice Huang’s romantic partner, people familiar with the matter said.

It is unclear how far along operators are in meeting their overall goal for that project, which at 800,000 servers would be on par with hyperscale facilities used by companies like OpenAI.

It is also unclear what mix of servers they plan to use.

The parameters they have outlined in construction plans reviewed by Bloomberg – specifically, the total processing power as compared to the energy input – would be extremely difficult to satisfy with chips from Chinese companies such as Huawei Technologies. 

Still, the smuggled hardware disclosed in the filings reviewed by Bloomberg is just a fraction of what they would need.

These documents only cover hardware offered as collateral for loans – providing a small snapshot of the operators’ ambitions, while also underscoring how some Chinese financial institutions, including with government ties, were aware that restricted hardware was getting into China and willing to lend capital on those assets. 

Bloomberg was unable to reach the leasing company that lent money to Shanghai Kezhan, nor Shanghai Innovation Bank, which in addition to the money it lent Shanghai Shuoyao, also provided a 200 million yuan loan to another company called Shanghai Longjie, similarly with restricted Nvidia chips as collateral.  

Shanghai Longjie – which has the same parent company as Shanghai Shuoyao – disclosed in documents filed to regulators that it has servers containing Nvidia’s earlier Hopper-generation chips, which are illegal to ship to China without Washington’s permission, Bloomberg reported in November.

That hardware was manufactured by Super Micro Computer and Dell Technologies. It is unclear whether the shipments had US approval.

Those are not the only Hopper chips at the Yangtze River Delta Project.

Shanghai Kezhan, the company that described the GB200 server in filings in 2025, also disclosed that it has 32 servers with H200 chips there.

These products had a Gigabyte prefix in their model name, but the documents did not include serial numbers – making them harder to trace. 

Shanghai Kezhan is headquartered about half a kilometre from the Yangtze River Delta Project, at the same commercial complex where Shanghai Shuoyao solicited engineers to work on Nvidia H100 and H200 chips – two restricted models.

In February 2024, both of these firms added “imports and exports” to their business activities, according to data from Qizhidao, a company information provider.  

The same month, Megaspeed’s original parent – the Chinese gaming giant 7Road – obtained 16.7 per cent of Shanghai Kezhan via a subsidiary the gaming company bought from Alice Huang in 2019.

The other 83.3 per cent of Kezhan is ultimately owned by NeXPower Japan, according to Qizhidao.

Japan’s official companies registry returned only one company named NeXPower, which was established in March 2025. Caixin, a Chinese business news outlet, said the Tokyo firm is controlled by Alice Huang.

Bloomberg has been unable to reach NeXPower for comment.

Chinese-speaking staffers at the firm’s registered address would not confirm that was NeXPower’s office, and shut the door after Bloomberg News asked about their relationship with Alice Huang and Shanghai Kezhan.

On the intercom was a message saying they are working and will not respond to media questions. The registered address of the company’s director appeared to be a vacated residence.

In May 2025, records compiled by Big Trade Data show, Shanghai Kezhan received a shipment worth US$11 million, flown from Malaysia to Shanghai Pudong International Airport with the company as consignee.

The customs document described the shipment as “storage chassis”, referring to a structure that houses components of a storage server.

But the product code it was assigned to was 847150, which denotes computing servers. The shipment’s unit price was US$264,108, too costly for a storage chassis – but within the price range of servers powered by Nvidia’s Hopper chips. BLOOMBERG

These processors were until recently Nvidia’s most powerful data centre products, and they have always been illegal to ship to China without a US licence. 

US President Donald Trump has explicitly said he does not want these chips – which OpenAI and Anthropic use to train their most cutting-edge models – going to the Asian country, at least for now.

Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang, meanwhile, once claimed they were too big to smuggle: a standard 2 m-tall GB300 NVL72 server rack, which contains 72 Blackwell Ultra chips and 36 Grace processors, can weigh more than 1,500 kg and is about the size of a gigantic fridge.

Nvidia and its just-reinstated CEO have come under intense scrutiny in recent weeks for their failure to stop diversion of the company’s products to China, a shadow trade that US officials believe is worth billions of dollars. 

It is unclear how the GB300 rack made its way to the country, to Shanghai Shuoyao or to this specific site – described in local media as designed to house as many as 800,000 servers.

By inputting the serial number for the product into a public warranty database, Bloomberg found that it was manufactured by Taiwan’s Gigabyte Technology, which assembles Nvidia chips into servers and racks.

The database also provided a model name for the serial number, which matches a GB300 NVL72 server rack manufactured by the Taiwanese company. 

This sort of gear often passes through several hands – including local distribution networks – before it is installed in data centres. In many cases, products that were ultimately smuggled into China were originally sold to parties in unrestricted areas. 

Bloomberg provided the rack’s serial number to Gigabyte, seeking information about to whom Gigabyte had originally sold the hardware and when. It declined to answer those questions, citing company policy.

The firm “conducts all business in compliance with applicable laws and regulations”, a spokesperson said in an emailed statement. “All transactions are subject to our internal compliance requirements and the relevant laws and regulations in effect at the time.”

Shanghai Shuoyao – the company that procured the GB300 rack and offered it as collateral – is active at the data centre linked to Alice Huang and also has significant overlap with Singapore-based Megaspeed, which is under US investigation over concerns that it smuggled Nvidia chips to China, Bloomberg has reported.

Shanghai Shuoyao, which has not responded to Bloomberg queries over the past year, confirmed in November in a rare public statement that it is one of Megaspeed’s service providers, describing the partnership as “limited to ordinary commercial cooperation”.

Megaspeed, meanwhile, used a rendering of the Yangtze River Delta Project in 2024 to describe its largest data centre to investors, dubbing the site a “specific area” facility in an unnamed country.

Bloomberg does not have evidence that Megaspeed itself diverted Nvidia hardware there, and Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing in response to the US probe.

The company has not answered repeated queries about the Yangtze River Delta Project. Nor has Nvidia, which for years insisted that there was no black market for its products and did not respond to questions for this story. 

The Trump administration in November put Megaspeed on a US trade blacklist, citing a significant risk of involvement in chip diversion.

Alice Huang in 2023 founded Megaspeed, a so-called neocloud that won a coveted stamp of approval from Nvidia within four days of its creation, and went on to become the chipmaker’s largest South-east Asian customer.

She also has ties to a number of companies that invested in the Yangtze River Delta Project, which counts Kang Wei as its president. Kang has been introduced at times as Alice Huang’s romantic partner, people familiar with the matter said.

It is unclear how far along operators are in meeting their overall goal for that project, which at 800,000 servers would be on par with hyperscale facilities used by companies like OpenAI.

It is also unclear what mix of servers they plan to use.

The parameters they have outlined in construction plans reviewed by Bloomberg – specifically, the total processing power as compared to the energy input – would be extremely difficult to satisfy with chips from Chinese companies such as Huawei Technologies. 

Still, the smuggled hardware disclosed in the filings reviewed by Bloomberg is just a fraction of what they would need.

These documents only cover hardware offered as collateral for loans – providing a small snapshot of the operators’ ambitions, while also underscoring how some Chinese financial institutions, including with government ties, were aware that restricted hardware was getting into China and willing to lend capital on those assets. 

Bloomberg was unable to reach the leasing company that lent money to Shanghai Kezhan, nor Shanghai Innovation Bank, which in addition to the money it lent Shanghai Shuoyao, also provided a 200 million yuan loan to another company called Shanghai Longjie, similarly with restricted Nvidia chips as collateral.  

Shanghai Longjie – which has the same parent company as Shanghai Shuoyao – disclosed in documents filed to regulators that it has servers containing Nvidia’s earlier Hopper-generation chips, which are illegal to ship to China without Washington’s permission, Bloomberg reported in November.

That hardware was manufactured by Super Micro Computer and Dell Technologies. It is unclear whether the shipments had US approval.

Those are not the only Hopper chips at the Yangtze River Delta Project.

Shanghai Kezhan, the company that described the GB200 server in filings in 2025, also disclosed that it has 32 servers with H200 chips there.

These products had a Gigabyte prefix in their model name, but the documents did not include serial numbers – making them harder to trace. 

Shanghai Kezhan is headquartered about half a kilometre from the Yangtze River Delta Project, at the same commercial complex where Shanghai Shuoyao solicited engineers to work on Nvidia H100 and H200 chips – two restricted models.

In February 2024, both of these firms added “imports and exports” to their business activities, according to data from Qizhidao, a company information provider.  

The same month, Megaspeed’s original parent – the Chinese gaming giant 7Road – obtained 16.7 per cent of Shanghai Kezhan via a subsidiary the gaming company bought from Alice Huang in 2019.

The other 83.3 per cent of Kezhan is ultimately owned by NeXPower Japan, according to Qizhidao.

Japan’s official companies registry returned only one company named NeXPower, which was established in March 2025. Caixin, a Chinese business news outlet, said the Tokyo firm is controlled by Alice Huang.

Bloomberg has been unable to reach NeXPower for comment.

Chinese-speaking staffers at the firm’s registered address would not confirm that was NeXPower’s office, and shut the door after Bloomberg News asked about their relationship with Alice Huang and Shanghai Kezhan.

On the intercom was a message saying they are working and will not respond to media questions. The registered address of the company’s director appeared to be a vacated residence.

In May 2025, records compiled by Big Trade Data show, Shanghai Kezhan received a shipment worth US$11 million, flown from Malaysia to Shanghai Pudong International Airport with the company as consignee.

The customs document described the shipment as “storage chassis”, referring to a structure that houses components of a storage server.

But the product code it was assigned to was 847150, which denotes computing servers. The shipment’s unit price was US$264,108, too costly for a storage chassis – but within the price range of servers powered by Nvidia’s Hopper chips. BLOOMBERG

data.title: US dollar set for flat week, still close to 22-month peak
data.description:
THE US dollar was still close to its highest level in 22 months after a the tech rout drove investors towards safe-haven assets.

The dollar index started its rally in early November and hit a 22-month high of 104.53 earlier this week. It was last little changed at 103.80 and on track for a modest weekly rise of about 0.03 per cent.

US stock futures rose on Friday (Nov 27) as investors returned from the Thanksgiving holiday with renewed appetite for beaten-down shares, following a seesawing of artificial intelligence stocks this week as investors weighed more attractive valuations against persistent concerns about heavy spending on the technology.

“We expect the Fed to remain hawkish and the US economy resilient, and our multi-asset strategists remain upbeat on US equities and the AI theme,” said Daragh Maher, senior forex strategist at HSBC.

“The main risk to our view is that renewed market weakness could erode rate support, with no guarantee that safe-haven demand would again compensate,” he said, adding that December’s Fed rate forecasts would be pivotal to the bullish cyclical greenback story.

If the tech rout fades, investors may strengthen expectations of Fed tightening, boosting Treasury yields and the dollar’s yield appeal, even as improving risk sentiment curbs demand for the currency as a safe haven.

However investors remained cautious despite Friday’s sharp rise in US stock futures.

“The high-beta Australian dollar, Kiwi dollar and Norwegian krone are leading gains in G10, although the moves remain modest compared with their recent losses,” Francesco Pesole, forex strategist at ING, said.

“That suggests the forward-looking forex market remains cautious about calling an all-clear on risk sentiment,” he added.

A so-called high-beta currency tends to amplify shifts in global sentiment, outperforming when risk appetite improves and underperforming when it fades.

The Norwegian crown rose 0.25 per cent to 9.74 versus the greenback.

The Aussie dollar added 0.7 per cent to US$0.667, finding its feet after dipping to a one-year low of US$0.6559 on Wednesday.

The New Zealand dollar was also supported by results of the general election, which reduced political uncertainty, even with no clear winner.

Geopolitics remained in the background but oil prices were on track to snap a three-week losing streak following attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and Saudi energy infrastructure.

Higher Brent crude futures often underpin the greenback against the euro and yen, as they boost revenues for US energy exporters while increasing import costs for the eurozone and Japan.

The euro was roughly unchanged at US$1.0964 with investors showing little reaction to news that Spain’s Pablo Hernandez de Cos was set to be nominated as the head of the European Central Bank.

Dollar/ yen 160 level back in focus

The US currency was steady at 159.27 yen amid concerns about another round of Japanese intervention.

Data showed that annual core inflation in Tokyo accelerated in November at the fastest pace in 16 months, bolstering the case for an interest rate hike as soon as December.

“The yen is understandably weaker today given the strong rebound in risk that has helped lift US Treasury bond yields,” Derek Halpenny, strategist at MUFG, said.

“Better risk conditions could quickly bring back focus on intervention especially if we get a hawkish hike from the FOMC on Dec 9.”

Benchmark 10-year US Treasury yields rose 5 basis points to 4.9 per cent. REUTERS

data.title: Greater economic integration, peace will be success markers for S’pore as Asean chair: Vivian
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Singapore’s upcoming Asean chairmanship can be considered a success if the bloc’s 11 members stay in relative peace and security, and it makes more progress on economic integration, said Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan.

On the economic front, Asean has not yet fulfilled its vision of becoming a single market and investment zone, he said during the closing dialogue of SPH Media’s Asia Future Summit on Friday (Nov 27).

There will be challenges negotiating the agreements needed to make this happen, including lowering trade barriers and committing to building a shared power grid, Balakrishnan said.

“But clearly, we need to do that,” he added in response to a question on what would mark a successful year for the Republic as chair of the regional grouping.

Singapore will assume the role, which rotates annually among the bloc’s 11 member states , in 2027 – taking over from the Philippines.

The Republic wants to maintain Asean as an open, inclusive engagement zone, but not allow the region to become an arena of proxy wars, he said at the dialogue moderated by Ravi Velloor, a senior columnist from The Straits Times.

“We don’t want to be forced to choose, but we want to engage all sides.”

The grouping’s 11 nations have different levels of economic and political dependency on the superpowers, he said, referring to the US and China.

But the bloc has “great potential” as long as it can stay open and inclusive, trade with and attract investments from the world, and run a “fair and honest system”, Balakrishnan added.

“That’s what success is in the medium-to-long term,” he said, adding that Singapore will do its part to move this along.

On the political front, the bloc needs to maintain Asean centrality – referring to the diplomatic doctrine the states subscribe to, which defines the regional grouping as the primary platform to drive South-east Asia’s politics.

“We will have squabbles, we will have disagreements, but our shared vulnerabilities far exceed our differences,” he said.

“Just keeping the 11 of us together in relative peace and security is the first success factor.”

Asean has come a long way since its founding in 1967, Balakrishnan noted.

Then, many of its member states had ongoing disputes and in some cases, recent open conflict including the Konfrontasi where Indonesian commandos bombed MacDonald House in Singapore, killing civilians.

“We’ve made tremendous progress,” Balakrishnan said, despite the ongoing civil war in Myanmar and a border dispute between Cambodia and Thailand.

The minister was also asked to weigh in on another ongoing issue: competing territorial claims in the South China Sea.

A set of rules for managing relations between Asean and China in the area, known as the Code of Conduct (COC), has been proposed, with negotiations meant to conclude by the end of 2026.

In an update earlier in November during the 2026 Asean summit in Manila, Philippine Foreign Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro said Asean and China have reached provisional agreement on about 80 per cent of the COC.

The South China Sea has strategic significance for China, Balakrishnan said, and Asean nations need to be realistic about this.

He noted that the Asean states which have overlapping claims with China in the area – Brunei, Malaysia, the Philippines, and Vietnam – also have overlapping disputes with each other.

There are difficult aspects to the negotiations, including a lack of consensus over the geographical scope of the disagreements in the first place.

There are also disagreements on whether the COC will be legally binding, he added. “These are very sensitive and difficult topics which we will need to work to get through.”

The issue has been discussed since at least 2018 – the last time Singapore was Asean chair, he added. “So it’s come down one full circle. All I would say is, we will do our best to try to move things along.”

The main considerations are to keep the peace and keep trade flowing, he said.

On China’s rivalry with the US, and how small states like Singapore can deal with it, he offered two rules.

The first, he said, is “try your best to stay out of trouble”.

The second is to engage all powers – but the question is how.

“I do not believe it is for Singapore to go around saying ‘yes sir, yes sir, three bags full’ in Beijing, then in Washington, and then in London or Paris,” Balakrishnan said.

Instead, the city-state must be consistent in its message: that it is not looking for handouts or subsidies.

“What we want is access. We want access to technology. We want access to your markets. We want to be treated fairly, and we want to be useful but not made use of,” he said.

Singapore must “play the game straight”, with a realistic assessment of its vulnerabilities and strengths, he said.

In response to a question on whether there has been a fundamental shift in Singapore’s relationship with the US, Balakrishnan said all relationships evolve, and that the US has been a vital, essential and stalwart partner.

Singapore has benefited from both America and China, he said, adding that the question is what happens when both “actually have a fracture”.

The Republic needs to have an honest relationship with both, and to reassure both sides that while it does not want to be forced to choose, it will not be used by either side as a tool against the other.

“It’s not a question of balance. That’s why maintaining a principled, consistent foreign policy is so critical for us”. THE STRAITS TIMES
